As far as I can tell, docs#Subgroup provides tools for working with membership in the uncoerced Subgroup, membership in the carrier set, and membership in the coercion of the Subgroup to a Set (SetLike?).

This comes up for me now because I have a proof of x ∈ ↑H in my context and rw [← H.inv_mem_iff] doesn't work. I'm pretty confident that membership in the coercion is identical with membership in the carrier, but rw [mem_carrier] doesn't work either. If a mem_coe theorem exists, I didn't find it.

So, some questions:

  1. If a convenience theorem exists for converting between two representations of Subgroup membership, is it considered a bug to any degree if an analogous theorem is missing for the third representation?
  2. Is there an established convention for how proofs in this area "should" be done? I've been using (H : Set G) everywhere even though it's harder to type than H.carrier, because I felt it was closer to what I really wanted to say and the representation in the context looks better.
  3. Wrt mem_carrier not working, I know that rw isn't supposed to apply equality-by-definition, and that's my best guess for why mem_carrier doesn't rewrite membership-in-the-coercion. But I've seen rw succeed in cases where equality-by-definition is required. I don't have an example to hand, but I think these are cases that look like rw [thm1, thm2 a, thm3], and the a I provide is equal-by-definition to what thm2 wants. I'd like to know more about this.
The question here is probable how you ended up with x ∈ ↑H in the first place. Anyway you can always do something like change x ∈ H at h (assuming h is the name of the hypothesis).
you can rw [SetLike.mem_coe]
you should never see Subgroup.carrier in your tactic state

Riccardo Brasca said:

The question here is probably how you ended up with x ∈ ↑H in the first place.

I'm working with cosets of a subgroup. https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib4_docs/Mathlib/GroupTheory/Coset/Basic.html

The notation is defined for sets, which is fine with me, but there is no automatic coercion of a Subgroup to its carrier set, so I've had to write a • (H : Set G) everywhere instead of writing the vastly preferable a • H. I actually complained about this in the last thread I posted.

Is there a better way?
Hmm, I see.

but there is no automatic coercion of a Subgroup to its carrier set

Strictly spealing the fact that (_ : _) works means that there is an automatic coercion, lean just can't work out what you want to coerce to without it

re: needing to coerce the subgroup to a set every time, I suppose you could define an instance like this:

instance {α β γ : Type*} [SetLike α β] [SMul γ β] : HSMul γ α (Set β) :=
⟨fun x S => x • (S : Set β)⟩

(though I suspect it's not a good idea or else someone would have already done it)

Aaron Liu said:

you should never see Subgroup.carrier in your tactic state

Well, intuitively, I agree, but Mathlib seems to be going out of its way to push me toward that. It's a lot less difficult to type H.carrier than it is to coerce H. At some point, if you want code to be written in a certain style, you need to make following the style you want require no more effort than following a functionally equivalent style.
You might want x • S to remain a submonoid, so you don't want the coercion to set, like docs#Submonoid.pointwiseMulAction
@Aaron Liu are you confused about the instance or the parenthetical

Yakov Pechersky said:

You might want x • S to remain a submonoid, so you don't want the coercion to set, like docs#Submonoid.pointwiseMulAction

I don't get it. That can't be what I want, because x • S isn't a submonoid whether I want to think of it that way or not. It's just a random collection of elements defined by relation to a different collection that is a submonoid. (Or, in the general case, a different collection that also isn't a submonoid.)

For example, 4Z={…,−4,0,4,8,…}4\mathbb{Z} = \{ \dots, -4, 0, 4, 8, \ldots \}4Z={…,−4,0,4,8,…} is a group, and a subgroup of Z\mathbb{Z}Z, but its coset 1+4Z={…,−7,−3,1,5,…}1 + 4\mathbb{Z} = \{ \ldots, -7, -3, 1, 5, \ldots \}1+4Z={…,−7,−3,1,5,…} isn't closed under the group operation and therefore can't be a subgroup.

though maybe if it was low priority it wouldn't interfere? idk
We have pointwise instances scoped in open scoped Pointwise, you could imagine a open scoped CoeDownToSetPointwise

@Michael is the reason you're working with cosets of a subgroup because you don't want to follow the lean-idiomatic way of making quotient groups (quotienting out by an equivalence relation) and are attempting to redo the theory by explicitly making a type of cosets of a subgroup? If so then you might want to consider doing things the idiomatic way. "Cosets of a subgroup" are the way that mathematicians are taught to make quotient groups, but it's not the way that it is done in mathlib.

@Michael I was stuck by this quite a while too. Yesterday I found a reason: that there is no @[simp] above Subgroup.mem_carrier. The tactic simp sometimes struggles with.carrier. 

lemma mylemma1 (h : (g ∈ H))  :  g ∈ (H : Set G):= by
  simp?

its route is 'Try this : [apply] simp only [SetLike.mem_coe]'

lemma mylemma (h : (g ∈ H)) : g ∈ H.carrier := by
  simp?

the route is 'Try this: [apply] simp only [Subsemigroup.mem_carrier, Submonoid.mem_toSubsemigroup, Subgroup.mem_toSubmonoid]'

Is this is helpful for you?

In a more sophisticated example, simp fails to solve the .carrier version but succeeds in the ( : Set G). After looking around, I think it is reasonable to add a @[simp] for Subgroup.mem_carrier. Why does Subsemigroup.mem_carrier have the @[simp] privilege but not his twin brother Subgroup.mem_carrier?

Kevin Buzzard said:

Michael is the reason you're working with cosets of a subgroup because you don't want to follow the lean-idiomatic way of making quotient groups (quotienting out by an equivalence relation) and are attempting to redo the theory by explicitly making a type of cosets of a subgroup? If so then you might want to consider doing things the idiomatic way. "Cosets of a subgroup" are the way that mathematicians are taught to make quotient groups, but it's not the way that it is done in mathlib.

@Kevin Buzzard I am only very indirectly attempting to redo the theory of quotient groups. You might note above that I'm not assuming cosets have a group structure; in general, they don't.

I'm attempting to go through the exercises of an undergraduate algebra course in lean. I think appropriate scaffolding can make lean a valuable way for people to self-study mathematics.

It happens that this does involve redoing the theory of quotient groups, but that's more because it's generally accepted that this is part of a basic curriculum than because I want to do something with them specifically.

My general approach is to have some material implementing a theory from scratch, and then in later material working with that theory assume there's been a transition to using standard Mathlib stuff. My personal implementation of cosets used functions called right_coset and left_coset which simply have type Set (once both parameters are provided; the full signature of right_coset is {G : Type*} → [Group G] → (H : Subgroup G) → (g : G) → Set G) and I found that pretty easy to work with. But for all later material I am trying to use Mathlib's provided functionality, and for cosets it happens to be an ergonomic nightmare.

I agree with you that an undergraduate algebra course could well have quotient groups. What I am trying to point out is that an undergraduate algebra course also contains a set-theoretic model for constructing these quotient groups, and in type theory this model is unidiomatic.

If G is a group and H is a subgroup then here are three statements that you can make about the quotient G/H.

1) G/H satisfies the following universal property: to give a function from G/H to X is to give a function from G to X which is constant on cosets of H.

2) G/H can be represented as a set of sets: an element of G/H is a coset gH.

3) G/H is a set of sets.

My opinions on these three claims are the following. (1) is true and furthermore (1) is all you need. (2) is true and is a proof that quotients exist, but (2) is not useful (apart from perhaps in a pedagogical context for people who are not sophisticated enough to use universal properties such as (1) to develop a theory). (3) is false.

What I am objecting to is that you are saying "(3) is what the book says that G/H is, so I will insist on making (3) true". I am claiming that whatever the book says, (1) is all you need. Lean's definition of G/H is not (3), however Lean's definition of G/H does satisfy (1). Trying to make (3) true is actively fighting against Lean's foundational model, which is not set theory and is not really designed to make this "set of sets" construction, because you can't have a "type of types", the elements of types are necessarily terms.

Lean will provide to you a black box quotient G/H whose elements are not equal to cosets, however it will also provide to you a function π:G→G/H\pi:G\to G/Hπ:G→G/H and if you really want the coset associated to an element q∈G/Hq\in G/Hq∈G/H then you can have it -- it's π−1({q}).\pi^{-1}(\{q\}).π−1({q}). However this coset is not equal to qqq, and forcing this equality is idiomatic because it is reinventing the theory of quotients and you will lose all of Lean's inbuilt theory which works for the inbuilt quotients, most notably the fact that the proof that given f:G→Xf:G\to Xf:G→X constant on cosets, the proof that the induced map f‾:G/H→X\overline{f}:G/H\to Xf​:G/H→X satisfies f‾(π(g))=f(g)\overline{f}(\pi(g))=f(g)f​(π(g))=f(g) is rfl. This is not true for your unidiomatic model and thus your proofs will be longer and more idiomatic.

In short, I am suggesting that slavishly following a book is here a bad idea and that if you experiment with my claim that all you need is the universal property then not only will your life be easier but you will also perhaps learn a new and more powerful way of thinking about quotients, which will be more beneficial than sticking to the textbook.

I'm not following you. I'm not trying to make any statement about quotient groups here! I'm trying to make statements about cosets. Cosets really are sets.

You seem to be assuming that because I'm doing something with a coset, the thing that I'm doing must be defining a quotient group. That isn't the case.

Fair enough. I guess what I'm saying is that the lie that an element of a quotient is a coset is sufficiently pervasive that it might mean that people can overemphasize the role of cosets in mathematics.
interestingly, in mathlib the type of cosets is the same type used for the quotient group, it just doesn't have a group structure unless the subgroup is normal

the lie that an element of a quotient is a coset is sufficiently pervasive that

I don't know that I want to call this a lie. A close analogue would be the "lie" that a cyclic group is just modular arithmetic in the integers. It is!

That isomorphism is important because we know a lot about how to work with modular arithmetic. We may care less about the coset backing some element of a group that shares your universal property of quotient groups. But the equivalence is there.
When this idea was first presented to me, I remember finding it rather enlightening to work through the example of an alternative construction in this Mathoverflow post.
